questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: First and foremost it had to be at an ambitious university, since I wanted to try studying at one of these world renowned institutions. Secondly it had to be someplace far away, so that I could experience a culture very different from my own.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a very nice and enriching experience, but the academic aspects did now quite live up to expectations.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy. The university had made a really nice guide website, which had all the info you needed. A highlight included a timeline with loads of important deadlines! If anything it was almost a bit too much info, since the website seemed a bit daunting to begin with. However, it really was a great assistance.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not need any assistance, since the information was quite clearly laid out for me.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy to find, and it seems like the two main international dormitories are more or less guaranteed, even if the university doesn't say so. I stayed at Mejirodai International Village. It had pretty nice facilities, and an okay location for both campuses. Although it was slightly pricey, and the social aspect there is almost non-existent. The other alternative is on campus housing at Komaba International Lodge, which is cheaper, more social and closer to the Komaba Campus. Although it is a bit more run down.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Except for the Komaba International Lodge, there is no on campus housing.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They were very strict with what courses we could and could not take, and the rules and reasons seemed super arbitrary... They told us we were absolutely not allowed to take Japanese/English courses, unless we spoke fluent Japanese, but half the time Japanese/English just meant English (but asking questions or doing your homework in Japanese is also okay) AKA English is no problem! So be sure to ask professors, if they plan to instruct in English, and in that case take the courses you want in spite of any arbitrary instructions.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Very straight forward. There was a website with available courses for exchange students. Find the courses you want, go to the UTAS site and search for them, and press "Register" before the first week. For all my courses that was it, but for some more competitive courses there was a selection process. You could also drop any courses you wanted for the first few weeks, or even enroll in different ones, in case you changed your mind.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Very swift help by mail, and some open offices where you could go and ask.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not very, since a lot of them were changed between applying for the university and actually enrolling. Although, after figuring out Japanese/English courses were in fact okay, I got some nice replacement courses anyway.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be creative and make sure to try to apply for any course you like. Don't ask for permission, ask for forgivness.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The lectures where for the most part not very enjoyable, and there was a lot of aspects which my home university did better.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of the courses was extremely varied. Some where trivial first and second year stuff, while others where more geared towards graduate students. Since they have four year undergrad programs in Japan, many courses are open for both fourth year undergrad students as well as graduates, so the level can vary a lot.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: UCPH had way better teaching in almost all aspects, at least for my faculty. The lectures here were all 105 minutes long with no break, and only rarely any interaction between or with students. The assignments were confusing and sometimes poorly made, often with a distinct lack of connection to the stuff from the lectures. You are expected to take a lot of courses at once, so there is not enough time to read up on any one course, without getting behind in another. The exception is the language courses for learning Japanese, they were very nice.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Of the courses I had: Nuclear Physics, Particle Physics, Japanese Language courses and maybe data chemistry. They also had a lot of courses called "Global Liberal Arts", which sounded quite fun, but just not for my field of study. I heard the Women in Science course was quite nice.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Not many unexpected, but a lot of things were just slightly more expensive than I had first assumed. Especially travel is expensive, if you want to go anywhere far.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food and rent first and foremost. The cheapest option at my dormitory was rent at 2500 dkk, but then they tack on utilities and maintenance, so in reality the minimum is over 4000 dkk. Eating out is about half the cost of Denmark, but cooking at home on a budget is actually a bit challenging, and can quickly add up to more than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were loads of potential "circles" which you could join, but in order to get much out of them you kind of had to speak Japanese. They did have a few nice events aimed at international students throughout the semester, such as the International Lounge and various cultural events.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The International Lounge (Friday lunch at Hongo campus) was a great opportunity to meet other students, both local and international. Cultural events such as tea ceremonies and workshops were also fun as well.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There is too much to list here. Japan is full of stuff to do, Tokyo especially, and there is something for everyone, so it boils down to personal preference. One thing of note is that flights to neighbouring countries are super cheap, so it is also a great opportunity for a trip to South Korea or Taiwan.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: No problem, Japan is a nice and safe country, so it feels very comfortable.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It is unfortunatly quite difficult to socialize with local students. The absolute best way to do so would be to speak Japanese, and then to join a circle and make friends there. If you don't speak Japanese, which most of course don't, then the International Lounge is a nice place as well.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I spoke with some other international students, and there are almost three distinct barriers with the Japanese students. First and foremost there is a language barrier, since most of them don't speak much English. Secondly there is a cultural barrier, since our background and life is so different from theirs. Third is a personal barrier. There is a tendency in Japan, to stay within somewhat professional relations, which does make it difficult to build lasting friendships.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The politeness and respect for other people. The general level of safety and consideration of others' comfort.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
I would say try to learn at least some of the language, it is very fun and rewarding. And the earlier you start, the more you'll get out of it furing your stay. Also take a language course, since they are super fun.
Try not to stress about passing the courses. As far as I can understand, it is not supposed to be difficult at all to get at least a passing grade.
Make sure to travel and experience the country as much as possible.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is a lot of specifics.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing the country and learning the language.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Maintaining motivation for my courses and making friends.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
